talks.summary:
Speaker and Security Operations Role

Brett Andrews, Anthropic's incidents and intelligence lead, describes his team handling technical investigations, forensic tooling, incident command, and threat-intelligence partnerships across commercial and government channels.

Anthropic Context

Andrews explains Anthropic's public-benefit-corporation status and responsible scaling policy, which can block profitable model releases deemed unsafe. Claude is available via chat and API, enabling programmatic agent architectures.

Threat Intelligence Foundations

He frames threat intelligence as reducing the defender's information asymmetry—illuminating attacker location and capabilities so defenses can be reoriented efficiently, using a fog-of-war metaphor around organizational assets.

Market Limitations

A core problem is commercial threat-intelligence opacity: vendors sell one-size-fits-all feeds that break the tight collector-producer-customer cycle found in government intelligence. The talk proposes exploring agentic AI to build organization-specific intelligence, though the available transcript ends during this problem framing before solution details.

talks.teaser: P. Srisawang explores #OOTB2025BKK - Security Onion: Scaling SIEM.
talks.summary:
Team and Project Context

Thai researchers from a former APP/network lab describe over a year customizing open-source Security Onion 2.3 for enterprise SIEM scale, emphasizing engineering lessons rather than sensitive customer data.

Why Open-Source SIEM

They chose open SIEM for lower license costs, customization freedom, code transparency, community support, and horizontal scaling on Elasticsearch-style stacks as log volume grows.

Tradeoffs and Security Onion Choice

Open platforms demand skilled staff, lack vendor SLAs, and may need custom features. Security Onion was selected for its all-in-one network and endpoint visibility plus active community, with a disclaimer that commercial Security Onion Pro exists.

Enterprise Enhancements

The case study covers performance tuning, custom development to fill enterprise gaps, and ongoing challenges when building production-grade detection on open tooling.

talks.title: #OOTB2025BKK Agentic ProbLLMs: Exploiting Al Computer-Use And Coding Agents
talks.teaser: Johann Rehberger analyzes #OOTB2025BKK Agentic ProbLLMs: Exploiting Al Computer-Use And Coding Agents.
talks.summary:
Speaker

Johan (EA red team director; independent researcher) introduces Agentic ProbLLMs, demonstrating LLM brittleness—models misclassifying images and answering 1+1 incorrectly under adversarial conditions.

Threat taxonomy

He layers risks from bad prompting and misalignment through jailbreaking to prompt injection, where third parties control inference inputs (web pages, uploads), impacting confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Persistent compromise demo

Building on prior Trust No AI work, he showed ChatGPT memory weaponized via attacker-controlled content: infections persist in long-term memory, poll GitHub for C2 instructions, alter behavior across sessions, invoke tools, and exfiltrate data—partially mitigated recently for image-based exfiltration.

Agents

Defining agents as software that perceives, reasons, decides, and acts autonomously, he links them to Boyd's OODA loop and warns computer-use/coding agents amplify prompt-injection impact when adversaries influence the agent loop.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Johann Rehberger, red team director at Electronic Arts and author of the paper "Trust No AI," presents research on the vulnerability of agentic AI systems, specifically computer-use and autonomous coding agents. The talk investigates how adversaries exploit the reasoning-action (ReAct / OODA) loop using prompt injection delivered via untrusted third-party content like web pages, documents, and GitHub issues. Rehberger demonstrates real-world exploit chains across ChatGPT Operator, Anthropic Claude Computer Use, Devin, and Google Jules that achieve persistent command-and-control, data exfiltration, and unauthorized local command execution.

Key Topics:
- Prompt injection threat hierarchy (bad prompting, misalignment, jailbreaking, third-party prompt injection)
- Persistent LLM command-and-control and data exfiltration via memory and storage bypasses
- Exploiting computer-use agents (ChatGPT Operator, Claude Computer Use) for data theft and command execution
- Attacking autonomous coding agents (Devin, Google Jules) via multi-stage prompt injection and tool invocation

Technical Details:
Rehberger outlines the prompt injection threat spectrum, emphasizing that indirect prompt injection fundamentally compromises confidentiality, integrity, and availability. He demonstrates persistent C2 inside ChatGPT by injecting malicious instructions via a GitHub issue into ChatGPT's long-term memory. Across subsequent user sessions, the poisoned memory instructed the model to fetch fresh commands from an attacker-controlled GitHub repository, update its identity, and execute unauthorized tools like image creation. To exfiltrate sensitive memory data despite OpenAI's URL-safe restrictions, he bypassed domain filters using allowed Azure blob storage domains (windows.net), triggering the model to render images with exfiltrated strings embedded in URL query parameters. Transitioning to computer-use agents, Rehberger targeted OpenAI's ChatGPT Operator. Despite Operator implementing safeguards like inline confirmations and warnings on sensitive websites, he tricked the agent via a malicious GitHub ticket into visiting authenticated user sessions (Hacker News and Booking.com), extracting private account details (email, address, phone number), and pasting them into a form on a deceptive "string combine" site functioning as an attacker keylogger.

The presentation further reveals remote system compromise using Anthropic's Claude Computer Use, Devin, and Google Jules. Pointing Claude to a webpage containing an injected directive to download and run a "support tool," the agent followed the link, downloaded a compiled Sliver C2 implant binary to the local filesystem, located it using bash, made it executable with chmod, and executed it to establish a live reverse shell. Rehberger adapted human social engineering into an "AI ClickFix" attack: a malicious webpage prompted the agent to click an "Are you a computer?" button, which copied an operating system command into the system clipboard via JavaScript; the agent was then directed to locate the terminal icon, paste the clipboard payload, and press Enter to spawn a calculator. In coding agents, Rehberger analyzed Devin's system prompt, noting developer attempts at "prompt begging" (instructing the model not to leak keys). He exploited an automated "expose port" capability (similar to ngrok) through a multi-stage prompt injection payload, causing Devin to expose an internal development port to the internet without human approval and exfiltrate the generated access URL.

Key Takeaways:
Deploying computer-use and coding agents introduces critical attack surfaces that cannot be reliably mitigated through prompt-level defenses or model alignment alone. Sandboxing remains mandatory but insufficient if agents have direct access to local secrets, API keys, source code, or internal network interfaces. Security teams must implement strict human-in-the-loop validation for high-risk actions—such as executing downloaded binaries, opening local network tunnels, and transmitting authenticated session data to third-party endpoints. Organizations must continuously monitor agent terminal commands, browser actions, and outbound network traffic to detect hijacked execution loops.

talks.title: #OOTB2025BKK - The Power Of Powerlogs
talks.teaser: Sarah Edwards investigates #OOTB2025BKK - The Power Of Powerlogs.
talks.summary:
## Apple Powerlogs Overview

Sarah Edwards of iVerify presents "The Power of Powerlogs" at Hack in the Box Bangkok, exploring Apple's Powerlog database—a rich telemetry source for digital forensics and incident response on macOS, iOS, and related devices. Though her day job focuses on mobile EDR against mercenary spyware like Pegasus, this talk targets DFIR practitioners.

## Where Powerlogs Live

Powerlogs reside under BatteryLife directories on Mac and iOS filesystems. Current logs are actively written; archived copies may appear depending on acquisition method, offering days of historical device-activity data often overlooked in investigations.

## Forensic Value

The database records application usage, screen state, connectivity, and peripheral interactions at granular timestamps. Edwards demonstrates correlating user behavior, background process activity, and system events—material that can substantiate or refute alibis, timeline reconstruction, and compromise indicators on Apple ecosystems.

## Collection Requirements

macOS, iOS, and visionOS support stock-device collection; Apple TV, HomePod, and Apple Watch may need developer profiles installed via paired devices. Edwards references sysdiagnose bundles containing complementary debug artifacts. The database's depth warrants dedicated study beyond a single conference session.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 - How I Learned To Stop Reversing And Love The Strings
talks.teaser: Paolo Montesel details #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 - How I Learned To Stop Reversing And Love The Strings.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Paolo (known online as babush) presents "Big Match," a research proof-of-concept developed to identify open-source libraries embedded inside compiled binaries by leveraging extracted strings. Reverse engineers frequently spend days analyzing proprietary binaries only to realize they are analyzing open-source code linked statically into the target. Because manual string searches using standard search engines or code search tools can be noisy, fail due to nested static libraries, or omit parent packages, Big Match automates binary identification by matching binary strings against a massive database of GitHub C/C++ repositories without relying on machine learning.

### Key Topics
- **The Pitfalls of Manual Reverse Engineering:** Relying on ad-hoc string searching often misleads analysts when static linking nests one library inside an outer framework (for instance, identifying libsrtp within a VoIP binary while missing pjsip).
- **Dataset Construction via GHTorrent:** Utilizing GHTorrent dumps (specifically MongoDB exports processed with PyMongo) to access GitHub repository metadata, stars, and commit histories without hitting clone bandwidth limits.
- **Repository Deduplication Challenges:** Filtering forks and duplicate projects across thousands of repositories. The speaker discusses graph traversal edge cases, such as the `octocat/Spoon-Knife` tutorial repository being merged into the commit history of `LibreCAD`.
- **Vector Space Information Retrieval:** Treating extracted string hashes as terms and repositories as documents using TF-IDF weighting and cosine similarity.
- **Clustering Search Results:** Using spectral co-clustering to isolate distinct libraries present together in a single binary instead of returning redundant forks of the first match.

### Technical Details
- **String Extraction & Filtering:** Repositories were scanned using `ripgrep`, followed by custom Python string de-escaping and hashing. Common boilerplate strings degraded matching accuracy; empirical analysis showed that pruning the top 10,000 most frequent strings (such as generic error messages) substantially improved results while preserving useful signatures like `GIF89a`.
- **Data Pipeline:** The ETL pipeline was built largely using Bash scripts and standard Unix utilities, which provided surprisingly fast execution (building the search database in approximately one day).
- **Secondary Deduplication:** To address excessive RAM consumption (averaging 40 KB of RAM per repo and 23,000 strings per repo), repos of similar zip file sizes were unpacked and deduplicated using Jaccard similarity thresholds, stripping thousands of Linux and Android forks.
- **Search Execution:** In the web demo, client-side JavaScript extracts strings from uploaded binaries, hashes them, and submits them to the server. The engine runs a matrix multiplication of query vectors against the repository matrix, followed by spectral co-clustering to display top matching independent libraries.

### Takeaways
- Exact string hash matching provides an effective, privacy-preserving, 0% machine learning mechanism to identify open-source components, as the server only receives string hashes rather than proprietary binary files.
- The approach works reliably when target binaries contain distinctive strings and can be extended to magic numbers, version range detection, monorepo dependency audits, and malware classification.
- Future directions include integrating string matching directly into decompiler plugins (such as rev.ng) to enable function-level string matching and automatic symbol renaming.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 LAB - Automated Incident Response
talks.teaser: Valentine Mairet explores #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 LAB - Automated Incident Response.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this workshop session at Hack in the Box (HITB), speakers Valentine (Val) and Harjit from the GitLab Security Incident Response Team (SIRT) share how their globally distributed team automates end-to-end incident response workflows. Operating across APAC, EMEA, and Americas regions, the team uses automation to ensure 24/7 service continuity, combat alert fatigue, standardize triage and documentation, and generate operational metrics to justify team headcount.

### Key Topics
- **Broader Scope of IR Automation:** Automation extends far beyond investigation log dives; it encompasses detection engineering, alerting pipelines, incident management, handovers, documentation, and metrics generation.
- **Detection as Code & Deployment Pipelines:** Managing detections in GitLab repositories with review processes, standardized formatting checks via CI/CD pipelines, and automatic deployment to their SIEM (Devo).
- **User Attestation Module (UAM):** Automated outreach via Slack bots to prompt users when high-risk events occur (e.g., Personal Access Token creation). Alerts auto-escalate if unacknowledged within a set timeframe (such as one hour).
- **Shift Handovers with "Hogi":** Maintaining continuity across time zones through automated asynchronous handovers and sync issue creation in GitLab.
- **GUARD Architecture:** The GitLab Universal Automated Response and Detection system, which ties together SIEM alerts, Slack interactions, Tines automation workflows, and a custom metric database (metricDB).

### Technical Details
- **Tool Ecosystem:** GitLab acts as the single source of truth for issues, documentation, and CI/CD pipelines; Devo functions as the SIEM; Slack provides an interactive chat interface for engineers; and Tines serves as the no-code SOAR platform orchestrating actions.
- **Alert Lifecycle in Slack:** When a Devo alert fires into Tines, Tines enriches the event with metricDB data and threat intelligence before presenting an interactive Slack prompt. Engineers can acknowledge, reassign, convert to an incident issue, or close the alert while logging qualitative feedback (sentiment analysis and relevance scores).
- **Practical Lab Execution ("Tokenheimer"):** Participants constructed a workflow integrating a Slack slash command (`/nuke`) via a webhook into Tines. Tines extracted the token parameter from `web_hook.body.text` and executed an HTTP DELETE request against the GitLab API self endpoint (`/personal_access_tokens` / self API) to immediately revoke exposed credentials. In advanced exercises, attendees added GET queries against the `/users` endpoint to determine username and permission scopes before revocation.

### Takeaways
- Standardizing and automating operational workflows allows small, understaffed security teams to scale consistently without manual overhead.
- Capturing metrics directly during alert triage (true/false positive rates, engineer sentiment) provides data necessary to tune noisy detections and justify organizational resources.
- High-risk manual actions can be safely accelerated by blending interactive user attestation with automated fallbacks.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D2T2 - Take A Picture Of Your App Code: Android MRI Interpreter
talks.teaser: SungHyoun Song examines #HITB2023HKT D2T2 - Take A Picture Of Your App Code: Android MRI Interpreter.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, San, a mobile security researcher at the Financial Security Institute (FSI) in South Korea, introduces the "Android MRI Interpreter"—a customized runtime and kernel-level analysis environment designed to inspect Android application execution and bypass Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) mechanisms without patching app binaries or using detectable user-space hooking tools.

Drawing an analogy to medical imaging, the speaker compares traditional penetration testing tools (like ptrace, Frida, and IDA Pro) to invasive surgery with a scalpel, which triggers application defense mechanisms and requires significant time to bypass. In contrast, the Android MRI Interpreter functions like an MRI scanner, observing internal behavior non-invasively at the operating system and interpreter level.

### Key Topics
- **ART Execution Flow Modification**: Android applications mix Dalvik bytecode, ahead-of-time (AOT) compiled native code, and just-in-time (JIT) compiled code across cold, warm, and hot execution states. Because optimized native code is difficult to reverse-engineer dynamically, the speaker modified the Android Runtime (ART) code flow so that native execution requests are bypassed, forcing all execution through a custom interpreter.
- **Interpreter-Level Inspection**: By replacing standard ART interpreters (the switch interpreter and mterp) with the custom MRI interpreter, the system directly inspects Dalvik instructions, methods, program counters, and virtual register values stored in ART's `ShadowFrame` and `ManagedStack` objects without alerting user-space anti-tamper protections.
- **Taint Analysis and Call Graph Generation**: The interpreter traces target data (such as sensitive strings) across data manipulation and transfer instructions (e.g., `move`). By traversing historical frames on the managed stack, it reconstructs execution call graphs displaying where sensitive data originates (highlighted in red) and where it is subsequently propagated or used (highlighted in green), filtering out duplicate calls and dead code.
- **Stealthy RASP & Integrity Bypass**: To bypass anti-rooting checks, Google SafetyNet, and commercial RASP modules, changes were kept inside a custom kernel rather than modifying standard user-space Android Open Source Project (AOSP) frameworks. The kernel intercepts `/proc/cmdline` to report clean boot state parameters (`verifiedbootstate=green` instead of orange caused by OEM unlocking). A minimalist privilege escalation mechanism was also embedded directly into the kernel's `sys_execve` handler: invoking the standard, unmodified `/system/bin/sh` binary automatically assigns root credentials (`uid 0`, `gid 0`) without installing detectable user-space root binaries.

### Technical Details & Demonstration
To showcase the tool's effectiveness, the speaker analyzed a widely used messaging application ("watch"), focusing on its two-step verification PIN handling. After configuring the target application's UID and the test PIN string in a configuration file (`/data/local/tmp` via BusyBox):
- **Instruction and Register Logging**: Real-time logging captured the function names, Dalvik instructions, and virtual registers when the six-digit PIN was processed.
- **Call Graph Inspection**: Mode 3 graph generation traced the PIN's lifecycle across app restarts, discovering that the PIN was persistently stored and decrypted via Android default decryption functions from `SharedPreferences` upon each app launch.
- **Target Function Tracing**: Using the identified method name, the tool focused execution tracing on specific internal functions, proving unnecessary memory exposure of the credential without triggering the messenger's rooted environment restrictions.

### Takeaways
Instrumenting the runtime interpreter and performing stealthy kernel patches provides deep dynamic visibility while completely evading user-space RASP defenses. When asked how developers can protect sensitive credentials from this level of memory tracing, the speaker recommended avoiding immutable string objects (which persist in memory) in favor of byte arrays or raw pointers that can be explicitly wiped or overwritten immediately after use.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D2T1 - Hacking Into IOS’s VOLTE Implementation
talks.teaser: Rajanish Pathak details #HITB2023HKT D2T1 - Hacking Into IOS’s VOLTE Implementation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researchers Hardik and Rajneesh detail an architectural and implementation flaw in Apple's Voice over LTE (VoLTE) stack. The vulnerability affected iOS releases prior to 15.1, as well as iPadOS and watchOS, allowing attackers within a cellular carrier's network to directly reach and attack millions of Apple devices without routing through or being logged by standard telecom billing and call-inspection infrastructure.

### Key Topics
- **VoLTE & IMS Architecture**: VoLTE routes voice traffic as data over IP Multimedia Subsystems (IMS) and the Evolved Packet Core (EPC). Handsets establish an Access Point Name (APN) specifically for IMS, initiating registration via SIP over UDP port 5060 before establishing an authenticated IPsec tunnel to the core.
- **3GPP/GSMA Specification Deviation**: Standard 3GPP and GSMA guidelines stipulate that once an IPsec tunnel is negotiated between the User Equipment (UE) and the IMS core (P-CSCF), the UE must terminate or close the listening socket on unencrypted port 5060.
- **Direct Device Exposure**: In iOS's implementation (specifically within the `CommCenter` framework and `libIPTelephony`), port 5060 remained open and listening on interface `pdp_ip1` even after IPsec establishment. Furthermore, lack of strict traffic segregation at the carrier P-CSCF level allowed arbitrary devices to communicate peer-to-peer over the IMS APN.

### Technical Details
- **Test Bed Setup**: The researchers reproduced the issue in a lab environment using Open5GS (simulating RAN/EPC), Kamailio (simulating the IMS SIP server), USRP and BladeRF Software Defined Radios (SDRs) acting as eNodeB/gNodeB base stations, ISIM test cards, Android test devices, and iPhones.
- **Reconnaissance & Enumeration**: By scanning IP ranges allocated to the carrier's IMS APN via tools like Nmap, the researchers found that only iOS devices responded on port 5060, revealing millions of vulnerable endpoints. Testing against Android devices (Samsung, Google Pixel) showed that Android correctly closes port 5060 once the IPsec tunnel is active.
- **Exploitation & Impact**:
  - **Caller ID Spoofing & Ringing**: Unauthenticated, crafted SIP `INVITE` packets sent directly to target IP addresses triggered the native incoming call screen and rang devices without legitimate telecom routing or billing records.
  - **PII Leakage**: Device responses exposed device identities, exact iOS versions, phone numbers (MSISDN), IMEI numbers, and potential IMSI exposure.
  - **Denial of Service (DoS) & Fuzzing**: Direct SIP traffic floods could tie up the telephony daemon, prevent legitimate incoming and outgoing calls, and expose low-level telephony parsing libraries to direct network-level fuzzing.

### Takeaways & Mitigation
Following initial disclosure in March 2021, an early fix attempt by Apple was bypassed, leading to an effective resolution in iOS 15.2 by properly closing socket port 5060 and strictly accepting SIP communication exclusively over the established IPsec tunnel. The researchers emphasized that adhering to core telecom standards is critical, as minor implementation deviations in foundational protocols can leave millions of endpoints exposed to remote, unauthenticated attacks.

This talk presents security research into Azure Machine Learning (AML) service, discovering multiple critical vulnerabilities in cloud-based ML infrastructure. The speaker, Nes from Trend Micro, structured findings across four chapters of investigation.

**Overview and Motivation**
The research began after observing a pattern of Jupyter Notebook-based service vulnerabilities across major cloud providers. The speaker investigated Azure Machine Learning—a widely-deployed ML-as-a-service platform underlying Microsoft's cognitive and applied AI services—revealing multiple classes of credential exposure and authentication bypass issues.

**Key Vulnerabilities Found**

1. **Credential Logging in Clear Text**: Storage account primary access keys appeared in Azure Batch startup task error logs and authorization logs. These credentials were also stored as environment variables (named PASWD) in agent configuration files, accessible because the default azure-user has sudo privileges without password requirement.

2. **JWT Token Exposure**: User authentication tokens appeared in URL parameters during Jupyter terminal requests and were logged in plain text in nginx access logs. These tokens could be captured via network traffic inspection and belonged to the compute instance owner.

3. **Network-Adjacent Information Disclosure (mlc)**: The DSi Mount Agent running as root exposed an unauthenticated API on port 46802 within virtual networks. Network-adjacent attackers could enumerate installed services and access their logs, including commands executed via sudo that contained embedded credentials for mounting file shares.

4. **Managed Identity Token Extraction from Non-Azure Environments**: The speaker demonstrated that certificate and private key files from compute instances, combined with environment variable configurations, enabled extraction of Azure AD tokens for managed identities from outside Azure environments. This contradicted documented design principles stating only Azure resources should fetch such tokens. Both system-assigned and user-assigned managed identity tokens were obtainable.

5. **Persistent Storage Account Access After Key Rotation**: Even after rotating storage account keys, attackers possessing the certificate, private key, and environment files could continue accessing workspace secrets. The workspace automatically synchronizes new keys, making traditional rotation ineffective against this threat model.

**Technical Architecture Details**
Compute instances are managed Ubuntu VMs in Microsoft subscriptions running multiple agents for mounting, monitoring, and identity management. Authentication flows through Azure Active Directory to generate ARM tokens, subsequently generating AML tokens. Data stores use credential-based authentication (storage account name plus primary key) to mount Azure File Shares across all compute instances by design. The nginx proxy on port 44224 handles incoming requests and forwards them based on the XMS-Target-Port header without logging sensitive information.

**Compromise Chain and Risk Model**
The speaker presented a scenario where a single compute instance breach could expose: other users' notebooks and scripts (stored in shared file shares by design), storage account credentials enabling full workspace access, managed identity tokens for lateral movement, and audit trails that appear identical for legitimate and malicious access patterns.

**Research Attempts Without Finding Exploitable Vulnerabilities**
The speaker also explored container escape in Azure Jobs, cross-tenant scenarios, dependency confusion attacks, and Jupiter implementation misconfigurations (beyond JWT logging) without discovering additional vulnerabilities.

**Microsoft's Remediation**
Addressed issues included masking credentials in logged commands, preventing JWT tokens from reaching compute instances, restricting DSi Mount Agent port exposure through nginx proxy and certificate verification, and implementing additional authentication requirements.

**Key Recommendations**
Deploy through virtual networks and private endpoints, enable comprehensive cloud logging and monitoring, scope managed identities to least privilege principles, monitor for unauthorized certificate usage, implement threat modeling for cloud environments using frameworks like Atlas for AI systems, and follow defense-in-depth strategies acknowledging the shared responsibility model.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, speaker Chris explores the concept of building an autonomous, smart-contract-powered rootkit command-and-control (C2) infrastructure using blockchain technology. Traditional rootkit operations rely on intermediate jump boxes to evade attribution, but reverse engineering and infrastructure reuse often expose attacker origins. By leveraging smart contracts on networks like Ethereum and Polygon, an attacker can emit blockchain events to trigger commands on compromised hosts, drastically reducing infrastructure costs while hindering traditional forensic attribution.

### Key Topics
- **Attribution Challenges in Traditional C2:** Attackers typically place intermediate jump boxes between their true systems and victim machines. Incident responders and forensic analysts identify these jump boxes by imaging drives, reverse-engineering malware binaries, and identifying shared attacker infrastructure. Adding more hops increases attacker costs and complexity.
- **Smart Contracts as Anonymous C2:** Interacting with public blockchain smart contracts does not tie actions to an attacker's IP, username, or system identity. Unless attackers fund transactions via KYC-regulated cryptocurrency exchanges without obfuscation (such as mixers or testnet faucets), traditional blockchain forensics cannot easily identify the actor.
- **Event-Driven Execution:** By invoking contract functions that log events (e.g., an `fx` event log), a rootkit running on a compromised host can monitor the blockchain, parse event payloads, and run local commands without establishing direct outbound connections to attacker-owned servers.
- **Countermeasures and Detection:** Organizations face significant challenges detecting these operations because interactions can run over ubiquitous protocols like HTTP via blockchain RPC services (such as Infura). Defenses require monitoring outbound connections for blockchain traffic alongside standard system hardening.

### Technical Details
- **Smart Contract Implementation:** The speaker demonstrated a contract written in Vyper (a Pythonic smart contract language) deployed using Ethereum Remix. The contract featured an admin management function and a `reporter` function that emits an `fx` event containing an address and an arbitrary string.
- **Rootkit Agent Architecture:** The victim-side rootkit connects to the contract's event stream. Within a function named `handle_event`, it extracts event parameters, verifies incoming messages, and executes operating system commands via standard system calls (such as `ls` for directory listings or shutdown routines).
- **Network and Testing Layer:** The live demonstration was executed on the Polygon (Matic) network due to lower transaction costs and faster execution. The speaker noted that testnet coins from faucets can be used to deploy and interact with contracts anonymously without financial or exchange footprints.
- **Two-Way Communication Concept:** While the primary demonstration focused on one-way command delivery via event logs, bidirectional communication is theoretically possible by assigning a wallet key to the rootkit itself and configuring it as an admin authorized to post return transactions to the contract.

### Takeaways
Using smart contracts for rootkit command-and-control introduces a powerful mechanism for evasion and anonymity that neutralizes traditional jump-box tracking. While no open-source or active in-the-wild exploitation tools utilizing this exact approach were known to the presenter at the time of the talk, defenders must recognize the threat and adapt monitoring controls to inspect outbound blockchain RPC and API traffic. Due to the high risk of malicious abuse, the presenter stated they do not intend to make the rootkit code publicly available.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this keynote address at HITB CyberWeek 2021, Matt Johnson, Chief Security Officer (CSO) at Ledger, examines the rapid expansion of alternative payment systems, cryptocurrency, and Web3 technologies. Framing the current landscape as a transition from an information revolution to a "revolution of value," Johnson compares modern blockchain adoption to the early days of the internet around 1998. He emphasizes that while adoption and transaction values are surging—particularly in rising economies and cross-border contexts—widespread hesitation remains, driven predominantly by security fears, scams, and a lack of user education.

### Key Topics
- **Web3 Evolution and Adoption Pace:** The shift from Web1 (open protocols, decentralized) and Web2 (centralized corporate platforms monetizing personal data) to Web3 (community-driven and decentralized). Crypto adoption is comparable to the internet in 1998, but accelerating at an even faster rate.
- **Self-Custody and Security Architecture:** Core crypto tenets including self-sovereignty, transparency, and self-custody ("not your keys, not your assets"). Relying on centralized exchanges means users do not truly control their assets.
- **Market Realities and Cross-Border Utility:** How rising economies (such as Nigeria and El Salvador) lead adoption out of necessity to bypass inflation and lack of traditional banking. Over 80% of crypto transactions operate across borders.
- **The Cyber Threat Landscape:** The surge in scam sites, phishing campaigns, blind signing risks in NFTs, and counterfeit hardware. Surfacing data shows that 71% of surveyed individuals view cybersecurity as the primary barrier to entering digital markets.
- **Developer Empowerment and Mass Education:** Why security must integrate directly into developer workflows via emulators and automated testing, and why mass adoption cannot succeed without broad public education.

### Technical Details
- **Endpoint Security Focus:** Blockchain shifts security focus away from network perimeters to endpoints, relying on four pillars: decentralization, transparency, self-custody, and self-sovereignty.
- **Hardware Isolation & Verification:** Ledger protects private keys by keeping them permanently offline (e.g., on the Nano hardware wallet or Ledger Vault HSM solutions for enterprise). Transactions utilize a "what you see is what you sign" model, forcing physical review of recipient addresses on an isolated secure screen to prevent address spoofing and blind signing.
- **Threat Intelligence and Takedowns:** Ledger’s offensive research team (the Donjon) analyzes ecosystem threats, noting that more than half of identified scam/phishing sites are registered via Namecheap. Ledger reports taking down over 500 scam sites (averaging 4 days per takedown, with a goal of 4 hours) and collaborating with platforms like Etherscan.io and Bitcoin Abuse to flag malicious addresses.
- **Vulnerability Research & Verification:** Emphasizing a "don't trust, verify" approach, Ledger engages in offensive research against competitors' hardware wallets, blockchain phones, and Hardware Security Modules (HSMs), while sharing findings, tools, and bug bounties (including phishing intelligence bounties) openly with the community.

### Takeaways
- **Security and Usability Must Converge:** Complexity is the enemy of security. Developers must be equipped with friendlier tools, emulators, and automated code review so security is built into Web3 applications from inception.
- **Mass Education is Prerequisite to Mass Adoption:** Just as early ATM users had to be educated never to share their PINs, crypto users must be taught never to disclose their 24-word recovery seeds.
- **Proactive Ecosystem Defense:** Securing the Web3 space requires an active industry-wide offensive against scammers, counterfeit devices, and malicious domains to lower the barrier of entry for mainstream users.

talks.summary:
### Overview
During HITB2021 Singapore (HATS D2), the host spoke with the engineering team from Techmaker to showcase the "ultimate hacker badge" designed for Hack in the Box events, including Cyber Week, Amsterdam, and Singapore. The team developed a modular badge architecture modeled as a "head" and swappable "hats." Instead of producing an entirely new badge for each event, attendees keep a core base board and receive or collect add-on hat boards that expand its capabilities across different conferences.

### Key Topics
- **Modular Hardware Architecture**: The base board (the "head") acts as the central compute unit, while plug-in modular boards ("hats") provide application-specific hardware. Physical interconnection uses a standard laptop RAM-style connector to lock the boards firmly in place without play.
- **Base Board as an IoT Hacking Target**: Designed conceptually like OWASP Juice Shop but for embedded hardware, the head functions as an interactive IoT learning tool featuring open-source firmware loaded with more than 10 hands-on hacking challenges based on real-world IoT security scenarios.
- **Supply Chain and Component Shortages**: The designers detailed how global semiconductor shortages (particularly impacting automotive and microcontrollers like the STM32 family) influenced hardware iterations, component substitutions, and stock reservations, ultimately validating their choice of the ESP32 platform.
- **Modular Hat Ecosystem**: Techmaker demonstrated and outlined multiple hat variants, including a CAN bus automotive sniffer, an environmental monitoring hat, and a multimedia/audio hat.

### Technical Details
- **Base Hardware**: Built around an ESP32 dual-core microcontroller featuring built-in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, an onboard antenna, and an additional 8 MB of external RAM suitable for tasks like audio processing. It integrates two round IPS displays (240 pixels each, resembling modern smartwatch screens) positioned as eyes, four capacitive touch buttons, an onboard lithium charging circuit, and an 18650 lithium battery slot for autonomous operation.
- **Interconnect Mechanism**: Connects the hat and head using a standard laptop SODIMM/RAM mechanical slot design, allowing hats to partially overlap the round displays for a layered 3D aesthetic while ensuring robust physical stability compared to standard USB or pin headers.
- **CAN Bus Hat**: Integrates a CAN bus transceiver and physical wiring connector, functioning as a bridge between an analysis laptop and vehicle networks, UAVs, or robotics using CAN bus. In automotive testing, it allows interacting with internal buses, analyzing traffic passing through security gateways (hardware firewalls isolating infotainment systems from critical vehicle networks), and identifying vulnerabilities in gateway implementations.
- **Additional Hats in Development**:
  - *Environmental Monitoring Hat*: Incorporates a Bosch BME680 sensor to track temperature, barometric pressure, relative humidity, and volatile organic compound (VOC) gas percentages.
  - *Multimedia Hat*: Features addressable colored LEDs (e.g., for equalizer/disco lighting effects) and microphones equipped with physical hardware kill switches for privacy control.

### Takeaways
The Techmaker badge shifts conference badge design away from single-use novelties toward an extensible, multi-event embedded security platform. By combining a resilient ESP32 core, open-source firmware, and mechanically secure SODIMM-based expansion hats, attendees can transition from beginner IoT firmware hacking challenges to hardware-level automotive CAN bus reverse engineering on a single device.

### Overview
This session is a post-talk Q&A from HITB2021SIN featuring security researchers Xingyu Jin and Richard Neal. The discussion covers practical aspects of vulnerability disclosure, Android platform defense strategies, the handling of bug bounty submissions lacking proofs of concept (PoCs), Google's fuzzing and crash triage workflows, and recruitment within security teams.

### Key Topics
- **External Vulnerability Submissions**: Handling vulnerability reports submitted without detailed write-ups or functional proofs of concept, and how bug bounty programs incentivize complete submissions.
- **Android Security Architecture & Defensive Mechanisms**: Initiatives such as the Generic Kernel Image (GKI) project designed to streamline kernel security patching across the diverse device ecosystem.
- **Memory Safety and Language Adoption**: Transitioning components from C to Rust across internal teams, applications, and potentially kernel development to curb memory corruption vulnerabilities.
- **Fuzzing Infrastructure & Crash Triage**: Methodologies for fuzzing on virtualized and physical devices across Android and Chrome, along with distributed workflows for evaluating crash exploitability.
- **Public Disclosure Philosophy**: The rationale for disclosing vulnerability details publicly to empower defensive security rather than leaving security in closed silos.

### Technical Details
- **Vulnerability Reports Without PoCs**: The speakers estimate that approximately 20% to 30% of vulnerability reports arrive without a proof of concept or reproduction steps. While experienced and frequent researchers usually include comprehensive reproduction materials, newer contributors sometimes supply minimal information (such as pointing out a few lines of code), requiring internal engineers to verify and construct exploit chains themselves.
- **Generic Kernel Image (GKI)**: Addressed as a central effort to unify the kernel baseline across Android devices. Centrally delivering a single kernel image reduces the per-tree maintenance burden for upstream security patches, allowing downstream devices to receive security updates much faster.
- **Language Transition to Rust**: Acknowledging that the Linux kernel remains predominantly written in C, internal teams are increasingly adopting Rust for applications and exploring it for kernel development to directly eliminate common memory safety issues, undefined memory accesses, and race conditions.
- **Fuzzing and Hardware Heterogeneity**: Android fuzzing utilizes both virtualized environments and physical hardware. A primary technical challenge in fuzzing Android devices stems from the high number of OEM-specific hardware drivers, where standard virtualization often fails. Fuzzing outputs and crash triage are not managed by a single monolithic team; instead, initial triage routes crashes to the relevant subsystem groups (such as Chrome, Android, or specific development teams responsible for the code).

### Takeaways
- Fuzzing and automated static/dynamic analysis must be paired with human code review, as complex bugs and non-standard driver layers often evade standard virtualization.
- Mitigating memory corruption requires systemic architectural adjustments, including memory-safe languages like Rust and centralized patching pipelines like GKI.
- Public disclosure of security research and vulnerability findings is viewed by the researchers as essential for fostering stronger overall community defense against malicious exploitation.

talks.summary:
## Overview
In this candid conversation at HITB 2021 Singapore, the Grugq—a veteran cybersecurity researcher and OPSEC pioneer—discusses his recent research into cyber theory, state-level cyber conflict, anti-forensics evolution, and practical operational security. Having worked in the field for over 15 years, the Grugq reflects on how threats have evolved, why foundational security principles remain critical, and why understanding attacker motivation and strategy matters more than obsessing over individual techniques.

## Key Topics

**Cyber Conflict Beyond Technicalisms**
The Grugq emphasizes that modern cyber threats operate at a strategic level beyond technical execution. He explains how state actors and criminal groups target not just governments but corporations to achieve geopolitical goals—citing North Korea's 2014 Sony attack as an example of successfully pressuring film companies to avoid certain content. He argues that ransomware, often dismissed as cybercrime, is actually aligned with state strategic objectives and should be understood through the lens of grand strategy rather than mere criminal motivation.

**OPSEC Fundamentals and the Three C's**
The conversation centers on practical OPSEC principles. The Grugq outlines the foundational "three C's": cover (maintaining plausible, legitimate explanations for activities), concealment (hiding activities from casual observation), and compartmentation (separating different operational contexts so compromise of one doesn't affect others). Effective OPSEC requires understanding your threat model first—determining what you're protecting, from whom, what the worst outcome is, and prioritizing defenses accordingly rather than attempting blanket protection against all possible threats.

**Multi-Device Strategy**
A key practical recommendation is the "one device per vice" principle. The Grugq stresses maintaining physical separation between personal and work devices, and between different operational contexts. He cautions against forwarding emails between accounts or mixing contexts, recounting an example of a US official caught because he forwarded emails between a secret account and work email, creating an unintended link that exposed him during investigation.

**Traveling Across Borders**
For international travel, the Grugq advocates "traveling naked"—crossing borders with a completely clean device containing nothing sensitive, acquiring necessary data only after passing through checkpoints. For those unable to afford multiple devices, he describes an iPhone technique: creating a clean iCloud backup, setting up a separate device from that backup for border crossings, and resetting to the real backup once across the border.

**Anti-Forensics Evolution**
The Grugq notes that anti-forensic techniques he pioneered 20 years ago—minimizing artifacts, operating in memory, using generic tools, brief operational windows—are now standard practices among sophisticated threat actors. He discusses modern evasion techniques like Gargoyle Lanterns, which toggles memory regions between executable and non-executable states to evade memory forensics tools that typically only capture executable memory. He also mentions process migration techniques that move malware between processes to minimize detection chances.

**Threat Actor Sophistication Gap**
A recurring theme is selection bias: detected threat actors represent only those who got caught. Truly sophisticated actors likely aren't using advanced techniques at all, instead hiding "in plain sight" through patience and minimal activity. Time is critical—if defenders have infinite time, they'll detect any intrusion, but if attackers complete objectives quickly, defenders must be lucky rather than just thorough.

**Device Security Recommendations**
The Grugq recommends modern Android phones with AOSP or GrapheneOS as generally more secure than typical laptops. He notes that location security is distinct from device security; phones inherently leak location data. Regarding network-level threats like Stingrays, he observes these are used but increasingly unrealistic threats given the prevalence of 4G/5G over older GSM/3G protocols, though neither are truly secure.

**Historical Perspective: Linux Kernel Compromise**
The Grugq references the 2003 Linux kernel.org compromise, which was detected through an MD5 comparison performed by a developer concerned about network reliability—pure chance that caught the attacker. He has obtained accounts from both the attacker and the kernel.org security team, noting that rebuilding from clean backups was necessary despite the apparent sophistication of the attack.

## Takeaways
1. Understanding cyber strategy and attacker motivation is as important as technical implementations
2. Effective OPSEC requires threat modeling before tool selection; generic defenses are ineffective
3. The gap between caught and successful threat actors is vast; publicly known techniques don't represent state-of-the-art
4. Foundational security principles—compartmentation, minimizing artifacts, brief operational windows—remain valid decades after formulation
5. Defense must account for both current observed tactics and theoretical vulnerabilities sophisticated actors might exploit
6. Financial motivation in cybercrime is legitimate resource allocation, not a sign of lower sophistication

# HITB2021AMS: Threat Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Application Security

## Overview
Ero Carrera, a 20-year veteran in infosec who spent the last decade at Google on large-scale malware analysis and threat intelligence automation, discusses the intersection of threat intelligence, machine learning, and security practices. He is joined by Dennis, another trainer, to explore both the opportunities and security implications of AI/ML in security operations, as well as application security best practices.

## Key Topics

### Threat Intelligence at Scale
Carrera highlights the fundamental difference between threat intelligence operations at Google versus typical enterprises: access to massive infrastructure supporting billions of rows of data across terabytes, enabling instant queries. Google's Threat Analysis Group consisted of approximately 20 people, including former government intelligence analysts, top reverse engineers, vulnerability researchers, and specialized threat analysts. While fresh data is crucial for tracking current attacks, maintaining historical context over years helps security teams understand threat actor evolution and infrastructure reuse patterns.

### Machine Learning Reality vs. Hype
Carrera expresses healthy skepticism about ML/AI, emphasizing that these techniques cannot do magic but excel at automating patterns within workflows. Approximately 90% of practical ML work involves debugging data—understanding incorrect labels, acquisition issues, sensor problems, and inconsistencies across tools. He advocates for interpretable algorithms (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Bayesian networks) over neural networks in security contexts because decisions often require justification for legal compliance and operational action. When stakes are high and actions depend on model verdicts (infrastructure sinkholes, etc.), the reasoning trail is essential.

### Feature Engineering and Expertise
Successful ML implementation requires both domain expertise and machine learning expertise working together. Domain experts understand data subtleties—what API calls mean, sandbox outputs, debugging approaches. ML practitioners understand algorithm behavior, overfitting, and parameter tuning. Carrera describes specific applications at Google: ML models for recognizing compiler patterns during disassembly at massive scale, and ranking evidence in threat intelligence workflows.

### AI/ML Security Concerns
Multiple attack vectors emerge:
- **Model Reversal**: Attackers can reverse-engineer black-box models to extract intellectual property and understand what the model knows, potentially revealing sensitive intelligence collection capabilities.
- **Oracle Attacks**: Repeated queries to a model can gradually extract information about its training data, especially problematic if the model trained on private or sensitive information.
- **Inference Attacks**: Attackers can construct computationally expensive inputs to cause denial-of-service on inference infrastructure, exploiting expensive code paths in model evaluation.
- **Data Poisoning**: False data or bias in training data can mislead models or hide malicious activity below the model's detection threshold.

Google's infrastructure includes options for resource limiting per inference job, though standard frameworks may not explicitly address such attack vectors.

### Application Security and Developer Training
Dennis emphasizes that application security repeats the same mistakes across decades—techniques evolve but fundamental vulnerabilities persist. The root cause lies in human factors; developers frequently copy-paste vulnerable code from Stack Overflow, import libraries with unpatched vulnerabilities, and lack security awareness. OWASP and security championship programs address this by targeting developer education rather than creating dedicated security experts. The key is moving vulnerability fixes left in the software development lifecycle (to code review phases) rather than discovering them late in release cycles. Developer security training differs fundamentally from attacker training: security is one feature among many for developers, requiring practical, code-focused education rather than tool mastery.

## Takeaways
- Infrastructure scale is a powerful enabler; advanced algorithms matter less than foundational tooling at enterprise scale.
- Interpretability and debuggability of ML models are often more valuable than raw accuracy in security contexts where decisions must be justified.
- Data quality and understanding dominate ML project timelines; poor data engineering undermines even sophisticated algorithms.
- ML models in security operations require protection from reversal, inference attacks, and computational DoS.
- Developers are the root cause of most application vulnerabilities; training programs should target development teams, not create isolated security experts.
- Moving security left in the development lifecycle through developer education is more cost-effective than late-stage penetration testing or bug bounties.

### Overview
In this 'Ask Me Anything' session at HITB2021AMS HATS, Andrea Zapparoli Manzoni, representing Crowdfense, discusses the operational realities, market dynamics, and ethical risk management involved in vulnerability brokerage and the zero-day market. The discussion touches upon how remote work and the pandemic affected exploit submissions, shifting target attack surfaces, operational lifecycle and acquisition procedures, and the pressing need for a standardized multi-dimensional risk framework across the offensive cybersecurity industry.

### Key Topics
- **Impact of Remote Work & Platform Operations:** Crowdfense experienced business continuity through its Vulnerability Research Hub (VRH). Despite the inability to host in-person events or network at conferences, researchers working during lockdowns submitted comparable volumes of research online, though some still resort to insecure channels like WhatsApp.
- **Evolving Attack Surfaces:** Major vendor platforms (such as mobile operating systems and modern desktop browsers) have significantly increased their security defenses, raising the barrier to entry for solo exploit authors. In contrast, IoT, SCADA, IP cameras, and SOHO networking gear remain heavily insecure. While Crowdfense primarily services law enforcement and intelligence gathering (excluding cyber weapons and industrial sabotage), interest in embedded devices is emerging where relevant to field intelligence.
- **Vulnerability Acquisition & Evaluation Lifecycle:** Crowdfense evaluates functional attributes, coverage, and reliability without requiring full upfront exploit code disclosure. Because reliability is paramount, fewer than 5% of submissions typically make it to operational field deployment. Crowdfense provides advance payments to review and test code, assuming the risk if an exploit burns or is patched during or shortly after acquisition.
- **Shelf Life & Market Metrics:** Reflecting on Crowdfense's 2019 catalog, 93 out of 125 intelligence-grade exploits remained unpatched zero-days by the end of that year. Long shelf lives reduce customer incentives to stockpile exploits.
- **Ethics, Integrators, and Risk Assessment:** Crowdfense strictly avoids selling to third-party integrators or intermediaries to maintain direct visibility over end-users. Manzoni argues that technical scoring systems like CVSS fail to capture broader societal, physical, and human risks. He advocates for an industry-wide, multi-dimensional risk assessment framework based on self-regulation.

### Technical Details
- **Submission Filtering:** Out of approximately 100 submissions evaluated, roughly five pass the strict filtering criteria covering edge-case stability, cross-version coverage, and low forensic artifact generation.
- **Shelf Life vs. Deployment Latency:** Integrating zero-day exploits into operational government or intelligence platforms often requires a lead time of one to three weeks. If an exploit is patched within a short timeframe (e.g., automated weekly browser patching), it loses operational utility entirely, whereas slower-patched systems may retain residual utility as n-days.
- **Risk Scoring Limitations:** Technical severity metrics like CVSS cannot accurately gauge real-world harm (e.g., an exploit affecting medical wearable devices versus typical software bugs).

### Takeaways
- Solo exploit development for hardened platforms is becoming economically and technically difficult, driving interest into poorly secured adjacent technologies.
- Brokerages must manage substantial technical and financial risks regarding patch unpredictability and exploit shelf life.
- Avoiding intermediaries and establishing multi-dimensional risk scoring are necessary steps toward responsible self-regulation in the private zero-day acquisition ecosystem.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Oguzhan Cakir (introduced in the transcript as Walshakaya), a Red Team Engineer at Picus Security, discusses the tradecraft of leveraging legitimate signed drivers—specifically older versions of the Process Hacker driver—to execute kernel-assisted post-exploitation actions without developing custom rootkits. By utilizing what he describes as "LOL-drivers" (Living-off-the-Land drivers), red teams can bypass user-mode controls, avoid API hooking by Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agents, and interact directly with Protected Processes Light (PPL).

### Key Topics
- **Kernel-Mode Motivations and Constraints**: Attackers turn to the kernel to evade user-mode monitoring, bypass access control lists (ACLs), and manipulate OS or AV components. However, challenges such as Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE), Windows PatchGuard, administrator requirement, and potential system instability (blue screens) make building custom rootkits difficult.
- **Process Hacker Driver Architecture**: Process Hacker deploys a kernel driver communicating via IOCTLs (Input/Output Control codes) through `NtDeviceIoControlFile`. While newer versions enforce a client verification key to prevent unauthorized applications from sending dangerous IOCTLs, versions prior to 2016 lacked this check and exposed sensitive capabilities like arbitrary process memory writing.
- **Hooking and Tool Adaptation via Microsoft Detours**: Red teamers do not necessarily need to recompile offensive tools to take advantage of LOL-drivers; they can inject a hooking DLL (such as one using Microsoft Detours) into existing tools like Mimikatz to dynamically redirect standard Windows API calls to driver IOCTLs.
- **Protected Process Light (PPL) Hijacking**: Windows uses PPL to isolate security-critical processes like `lsass.exe`. The speaker explores the PPL hierarchy (where WinTCB outranks Anti-Malware) to host offensive payloads inside protected processes.

### Technical Details
- **IOCTL Redirection**: Demonstrations show replacing `NtOpenProcess` (IOCTL 50) and `NtReadVirtualMemory` with `NtDeviceIoControlFile` calls dispatched to the Process Hacker device handle (`kphConnect`), effectively hiding standard API patterns from monitoring tools like API Monitor.
- **Process Injection & Thread Hijacking**: Using driver routines (`kphSuspendProcess`, `kphResumeProcess`, and memory writing) combined with thread context modification (`SetThreadContext`), a shellcode runner is implemented that avoids typical API hooks for `WriteProcessMemory` and process suspension.
- **PPL-Level Meterpreter Loader**: The speaker creates an early-bird injection loader that spawns a suspended `services.exe` process (signed with Windows TCB PPL level). Using the Process Hacker driver, the loader opens a full-access handle to this PPL process, writes an AES-encrypted Meterpreter payload, cues execution via an APC, and resumes the process. From this WinTCB-level `services.exe`, the operator migrates into Microsoft Defender's own process and successfully dumps credentials from a PPL-protected `lsass.exe` using Kiwi without error.

### Takeaways
- Utilizing signed, legitimate drivers that neglect strict handle or client verification allows attackers to execute privileged kernel-level actions while dodging DSE and PatchGuard.
- Converting standard Windows APIs into driver-specific IOCTLs normalizes or conceals malicious tradecraft from behavioral sensors tuned for typical user-mode API sequences.
- The speaker consolidates these implementations into an open-source tool called "Offensive Process Hacker" on GitHub and highlights future research into quieter driver installation methods.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Ilia Rabinovich and Oleg Lerner from Sygnia present Cloud Scout, an open-source tool designed to map and visualize attack paths across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. As organizations migrate traditional infrastructure to the cloud, threat actors exploit cross-platform connections, hybrid architectures, and expanding attack surfaces to pivot across environments and escalate privileges. The speakers introduce Cloud Scout to overcome visibility limitations inherent in existing siloed security tools by consolidating and correlating identity and asset data across on-premises, Azure, and AWS infrastructures.

### Key Topics
- **Hybrid Cloud Threat Landscape:** Over the last two years, organizations have accelerated transitions to hybrid and multi-cloud setups, interconnecting multiple cloud vendors, CI/CD pipelines, and microservices. Threat actors exploit this complexity by spinning up malicious cloud applications, targeting CI/CD workflows, developing cloud-dedicated malware, and leveraging cloud attack surfaces to pivot into on-premises networks or other cloud environments.
- **Siloed Tooling Limitations:** Existing open-source tools each address single-environment enumeration: BloodHound (by SpecterOps) focuses on on-premises environments, Stormspotter (by Microsoft) focuses on Azure, and awspx (by F-Secure Labs) focuses on AWS. Because these tools operate in separate databases, security teams previously had to manually consolidate data to identify cross-platform relationships.
- **Cloud Scout Architecture and Capabilities:** Because BloodHound, Stormspotter, and awspx all rely on Neo4j graph databases, Cloud Scout merges their data into a single unified database. It provides three primary functions:
  1. Connecting cross-platform entities (such as users, applications, roles, and services) based on corresponding attributes.
  2. Identifying cross-platform attack paths that threat actors could leverage for lateral movement and privilege escalation.
  3. Visualizing these complex, cross-platform attack paths within a single screen.

### Technical Details
- **Entity Correlation:** Real-world hybrid environments share interconnected entities. For instance, on-premises Active Directory accounts synced to Azure Active Directory can be linked between BloodHound and Stormspotter nodes using their user security identifier (SID). Cloud Scout enriches node data to construct both trivial and complex relationships across platforms.
- **Integration and Installation:** Cloud Scout is packaged as a plugin for BloodHound, downloadable from GitHub. Users install it by running a batch installation script. Once installed, BloodHound's interface displays additional UI buttons that handle the ingestion of data from the different frameworks and execute the logic needed to build cross-platform relations.

### Takeaways
- Visibility into interconnected hybrid and multi-cloud systems is a critical gap for modern security teams.
- Traditional assessment tools provide only fragmented views of specific environments, masking cross-platform lateral movement risks.
- By uniting data from BloodHound, Stormspotter, and awspx into a single Neo4j database, Cloud Scout allows defenders to uncover non-trivial attack paths spanning on-premises networks and multiple cloud providers.

talks.summary:
## Overview

Quark Engine is an Android malware scoring and analysis system developed by Kunu Chen and Jin Wei Sung. Rather than relying on existing cybersecurity approaches, the creators derived their methodology from principles of criminal law, resulting in a novel eight-principle scoring system combined with a Dalvik bytecode loader implementation.

## The Eight Principles

The scoring system is built on principles decoded from criminal law:
1. A malware crime consists of action and targets (similar to criminal definitions)
2. Loss of reputation is greater than loss of wealth (reputation is harder to recover than money)
3. Arithmetic sequence for penalty weighting across crimes
4-6. Order theory comprising three sub-principles: later stages indicate greater certainty of crime practice; more evidence increases penalty weight; proportional sequence (e.g., 2^n) reflects escalating severity
7. Crimes are treated as independent events allowing direct penalty addition
8. Threshold generation system to classify threat levels

## Android Malware Crime Order Theory

The core innovation is a five-stage theory mirroring criminal law stages (determination, conspiracy, preparation, start, practice):
- **Stage 1**: Check if malware requests related permissions
- **Stage 2**: Verify if key native APIs are called
- **Stage 3**: Detect specific API combinations
- **Stage 4**: Confirm APIs are called in correct sequence by tracing mutual parent functions
- **Stage 5**: Verify APIs handle the same register through CPU operation simulation

## Technical Implementation

The Dalvik bytecode loader implements all five stages. Stage 4 overcomes obfuscation by tracing function call hierarchies regardless of renamed wrappers. Stage 5 uses a custom "register object" data type storing register name, current value, and which functions access it. The engine simulates CPU operations line-by-line, maintaining a hash table history of register states to track data flow between APIs.

## Real-World Analysis

Two malware cases were demonstrated:
1. Non-obfuscated malware stealing location data via SMS with clear function names (send_message, get_location) containing native APIs get_cell_location and send_text_message
2. Obfuscated malware detecting Wi-Fi hotspots using get_active_network_info and get_cell_location APIs, with intentionally renamed functions (p.a, am.a, etc.) that still traced back to legitimate behavior patterns

## Detection Rule Generation

To scale rule creation beyond human capacity, a seven-step automated strategy was developed:
1. Crawl official Android API documentation
2. Ignore permissions in initial engine scan
3. Generate all possible API combination rules
4. Find first-stage verified rules matching actual malware
5. Add permission context from matched malware
6. Verify second-stage rules and count malware matches
7. Sort and review rules by prevalence

This approach reduces resource consumption versus generating all 1.26×10^13 possible combinations.

## Takeaways

Quark Engine provides malware analysts with structured confidence levels (0-100% based on stage evidence) for behavioral detection, enables rapid analysis of obfuscated code, and automates rule generation. Future work includes handling native libraries (.so files), packed APKs, API version changes across Android versions, and potentially replacing the currently-inactive Andrew Guard core library.

### Overview
In this talk, security researchers Gaston Guerra and Martin Oyanarte examine enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems—specifically Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS)—and how attackers can move beyond basic access (such as cryptomining or ransomware) to execute high-impact financial post-exploitation. Organizations rely on ERP financial modules to handle bank accounts, manage vendors, generate checks, and conduct electronic funds transfers (EFT). Despite handling hundreds of millions of dollars, many production ERP systems remain exposed to the internet and unpatched due to concerns that updates might break legacy business operations.

### Key Topics
- **ERP Exposure and Post-Exploitation Gap:** Many internet-facing ERP instances discovered on Shodan run unpatched. While attackers often compromise these systems for low-value goals like Monero mining, understanding ERP financial workflows allows direct monetary theft.
- **Thin Client Framework (TCF) Flaws:** Analysis of the TCF communication protocol, authentication bypass mechanisms via unhandled Java null exceptions, and remote method invocation via proxies.
- **Deserialization to SQL Injection:** Chaining object deserialization in `ServerPostMaster` with gadget services to achieve second-order SQL injection and modify backend database records.
- **EFT Wire Transfer Manipulation:** Intercepting and altering approved payment orders and bank routing details in the database before the automated payment close batch process runs.
- **EBS Payment Module File Upload & Remote Command Execution:** Exploiting the `fileDumpFunction` within `IBATransmitServlet` to write arbitrary files, upload a Perl web shell, and hijack the check printing process.

### Technical Details
Martin details an authentication bypass in EBS's Thin Client Framework (`APBS TCF servlet`). When a handshake request omits the `TCF-Start` header (making it null), calling `.equals("close")` triggers a Java null pointer exception that is not handled properly, allowing the session to persist and returning a valid `JSessionID` cookie without an EBS authentication cookie. Leveraging proxy classes, the researchers identify `ServerPostMaster`, which decompresses a zipped byte array into an `ObjectInputStream` and calls `readObject()`. By crafting a gadget chain utilizing `FNDMessageRequest`/`FNDMessageService` and `ContextBootstrapRequest`/`ContextBootstrapService`, they set the session's display language with a SQL payload. When calling `respond()` on `SingleResponseService`, the injected language variable triggers second-order SQL injection. By declaring a `pragma autonomous_transaction` in the Oracle database, arbitrary insert, update, or delete statements can be run—allowing the takeover of the `sysadmin` account and modification of approved payment records (updating bank accounts, branch numbers, and bank names) while clearing audit logs.

Gaston demonstrates a separate unauthenticated vulnerability in the `IBATransmitServlet` payment module. The servlet processes an HTTP POST request containing XML specifying a class (`fileDumpFunction`) and method (`transmit`), accepting parameters such as `fileDir`, `fileName`, and `transmitRef`. By supplying root (`/`) as `fileDir`, an empty string for `fileName`, and the relative target path in `transmitRef`, an attacker achieves arbitrary file write without path traversal. Gaston overwrites an existing Perl CGI script on the WebLogic server with a Perl web shell. Using a reverse shell connection to the reports directory, he locates a cached check file (`check.out`), modifies the payee and payment data to his own details, and executes `lp` to send the modified check file to the remote check printing queue, physically printing an unauthorized check.

### Takeaways
1. **Functional Controls Are Ineffective When the Core Platform Falls:** Once attackers obtain underlying database or operating system access, business logic validation and multi-tier approval workflows are completely bypassed.
2. **Blind Trust in ERP Integrity:** Banks and business operators inherently trust batch-generated EFT files and check spoolers because the payments were already approved by authorized personnel.
3. **Deserialization and Legacy Codebases:** Decades-old enterprise frameworks built with Java EE, reflection, and remote method invocation introduce severe modern attack vectors such as deserialization.
4. **Post-Exploitation Risk:** The security community and enterprises must realize that attackers will eventually focus on business logic and financial post-exploitation rather than commodity malware.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Łukasz Siewierski examines 'Zen', a complex multi-family campaign of harmful Android applications attributed to a single author or development group. Rather than analyzing an isolated malware family, the presentation explores the author's evolving portfolio over time. The campaign ranges from repackaged apps with custom ad SDKs to complex rooting trojans that automate Google account creation, click fraud, and system persistence.

### Key Topics
- **Custom Ad SDK Proxy**: Repackaged popular apps and fake mimic apps that route ad requests through a command-and-control (C&C) server, hiding the underlying ad networks and masking fraudulent activities from reverse engineers.
- **Large-Scale Click Fraud**: Automating ad clicks via JavaScript, Android APIs, or JavaScript interfaces. The malware parsed an unusually large 287 KB JSON list sent from the C&C server containing HTML keywords and corresponding JavaScript execution snippets.
- **Rooting and Fake Account Creation**: Downloading device-tailored exploits ('solutions') to gain root access. Once root is achieved, the malware silently enables Android accessibility services to automate the Google account creation wizard, using phone numbers and OTPs fetched dynamically from the C&C.
- **Code Injection and System Hooking**: Using `ptrace` and memory manipulation via `/proc/<pid>/maps` to inject code (`inject.so`) into remote processes. This mechanism extracts base64-encoded CAPTCHA images for remote solving and hooks system services using Xposed to suppress reboot requests and keypress events.
- **Persistence Mechanisms and Evolution**: Exploring four persistence tactics—modifying `/system/bin/install-recovery.sh`, copying binaries into `/system/priv-app`, swapping `framework.jar`, and injecting into `system_server`.

### Technical Details
- **Ad Proxying**: The custom SDK requests ads directly from the C&C server, which downloads resources from legitimate ad networks and proxies them back to the client, preventing analysts from identifying which ad networks are being abused.
- **Exploitation & Accessibility Abuse**: The client submits device hardware specifications to the C&C to retrieve a matching root exploit file. After gaining root privileges, it bypasses user prompts by programmatically updating `enabled_accessibility_services` and toggling `accessibility_enabled` to 1 in system settings. It then reads UI elements in the account wizard (such as 'enter the code' or base64-encoded titles).
- **Process Injection & Hooking**: The injector inspects `/proc/<pid>/maps` to calculate `libc` offsets for `mmap`, `dlopen`, and `dlsym`. It injects shellcode to run arbitrary methods within target applications, including intercepting `PowerManagerService.reboot()` to return 0 and intercepting key events (power menu, volume keys).
- **Obfuscation**: Certain samples embed encrypted payloads in the `assets/x/` directory using DES encryption, where the filename string serves directly as the DES key.
- **Mitigations in Modern Android**: Newer Android versions significantly disrupt this toolset. Verified Boot halts boot if `/system` files or `install-recovery.sh` are tampered with, or if `framework.jar` is altered. Furthermore, restrictions on the `/proc` filesystem introduced in Android Nougat block cross-process memory inspection, breaking the injection framework.

### Takeaways
The chronological evolution of Zen reveals an operational pivot: as rooting exploits became scarce, unreliable, and expensive across modern Android versions, the author shifted toward click fraud and dynamic code loading. Siewierski emphasizes that defenders must look beyond individual malware families to track the overarching goals, capabilities, and monetization pivots of malware authors.

talks.summary:
Patrick, a principal security researcher, presents an analysis of macro-based attacks targeting macOS systems through Microsoft Office documents. Historically, macro exploits (originating from the Melissa virus in 1999) predominantly targeted Windows systems, but as macOS becomes more prevalent in enterprise environments with Microsoft Office installed, attackers have shifted focus to this growing user base.

The presentation examines three documented campaigns. In 2017, a Trump-themed document contained malicious macros that execute when enabled by users. In 2018, a Bitcoin-themed document featured base64-encoded Python code that downloaded an Empire backdoor and Metasploit meterpreter payload, and notably included Adam Chester's sandbox escape exploit that abused a faulty regex to create specially-named files circumventing Office's file creation restrictions. In 2019, a Lazarus group document (attributed to North Korea) distributed an M1.T persistent implant targeting macOS.

For analyzing embedded macros, the speaker details using oletools (ole_vba command) to extract macro code from Office documents. Payloads are typically base64-encoded and executed via the auto_open subroutine when users enable macros. Microsoft's attempted patch for the sandbox escape was incomplete, still allowing file writes to parent directories of the launch agents folder.

The core contribution is a novel 0-click exploit chain leveraging XLM macros—an ancient Excel macro format from the 1980s still supported by modern Microsoft Office—which execute automatically even when macros are disabled. The chain delivers an XLSX file containing XLM macros that download a specially-crafted ZIP file, persists it as a login item (allowed from within Office's sandbox), and on next user login, Archive Utility unpacks it. Through clever path construction, unpacking creates a launch agents directory containing a plist file that launches daemon executes as a bash reverse shell outside the sandbox. The attacker can then install additional malware without notarization constraints. Detection is possible by monitoring for Office spawning curl/Python child processes and suspicious ZIP file login item persistence. Apple patched the vulnerability in 10.15.3; Microsoft's response was reportedly minimal.
